info.catalog_ids: Crennell 2 of 59 · Du Val B · Wenninger 26 · Wheeler 2 · DU30 · Brückner Taf. VIII, Fig. 2
history: The outer shape of this solid is by far the oldest thing on Brückner's plates. Around 1498 in Milan, Leonardo da Vinci drew some sixty polyhedra for Luca Pacioli's Divina proportione (printed in Venice in 1509), among them an icosahedron with a triangular pyramid erected on every face — the "icosahedron elevatum". But Leonardo's spikes are built from equilateral triangles, which makes them strictly taller than a stellation allows. The true first stellation fixes each pyramid's apex exactly where the three neighbouring face planes of the icosahedron meet: the three lateral triangles are then isosceles, each lying flat in a neighbouring face plane, and the coplanar triples fuse into twenty equilateral (but not regular) hexagons with angles alternating about 104.5° and 135.5°. A third, convex cousin — the Catalan triakis icosahedron, Eugène Catalan's 1865 dual of the truncated dodecahedron — has shallower pyramids still. Three different solids share one plan, which is why the name "triakis icosahedron" needs a warning label whenever it appears.

As a stellation the figure belongs to the nineteenth century. Kepler had edge-stellated the icosahedron in 1619 (producing the great stellated dodecahedron, not this solid), and Augustin-Louis Cauchy's 1812/13 memoir knew the great icosahedron and — on Guy Inchbald's reading — the regular compounds as stellations of the icosahedron; but none of that touches the modest first stellation. The standard modern account credits Edmund Hess of Marburg, whose 1876 treatise on simultaneously isogonal and isohedral polyhedra (published in Kassel) introduced the "complete figure" — the stellation diagram — and with it, Wikipedia's history of The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra says, the remaining mainline stellations of the icosahedron, this one included. Brückner's own footnotes point the diagram method straight at Hess's 1876 pages. In 1900 the Bautzen schoolmaster built the paper model and photographed it (Taf. VIII, Fig. 2); in 1924 A. H. Wheeler of Worcester, Massachusetts listed it at the Toronto International Mathematical Congress as his form No. 2, "hexagonal"; in 1938 Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie made it stellation B — the second entry of what became, in Kate and David Crennell's 1999 numbering, 2 of the 59.

The solid's second identity was also spotted first by Brückner. In §150 of Vielecke und Vielflache he presents it explicitly as the reciprocal of the small ditrigonal icosidodecahedron, a uniform star polyhedron of twelve pentagrams and twenty triangles that he photographs on the neighbouring plate (Fig. 15, Taf. IX) — noting that the dual's faces are equilateral hexagons with alternately equal angles, its core an icosahedron, and its 32 vertices those of an icosahedron and a dodecahedron together. That is precisely its modern status as a uniform dual, DU30, sixty years before the dual-model literature existed. Magnus Wenninger built it twice: in Polyhedron Models (1971) as model 26, the "triakisicosahedron", first of his seventeen icosahedron stellations, and in Dual Models (1983) as the dual of his W70. The now-standard name "small triambic icosahedron" comes from that dual tradition: Norman W. Johnson, who named the uniform star polyhedra and their duals for Wenninger's books, called the face a "triambus" — an equilateral hexagon with threefold rather than sixfold symmetry — and the small/medial/great triambic icosahedra are the three star duals bounded by such faces.

So the one solid carries three names from three centuries — Leonardo's elevated icosahedron (almost: his is spikier), Hess and Brückner's first stellation, and Johnson's small triambic icosahedron — and which name you use depends on whether you read its surface as sixty triangles, as a cell-set over the icosahedron's twenty planes, or as twenty intersecting hexagons. As a star polyhedron it has 20 faces, 60 edges and 32 vertices (Euler characteristic −8), with most of every hexagon buried inside the body; only shallow spikes show, the apexes standing barely 7% farther from the centre than the icosahedron's own vertices. That reticence made it the traditional first exercise of stellation — the smallest step off the icosahedron that the twenty planes permit.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner shows the model as Fig. 2 on photographic plate VIII, and treats the solid twice in the text. In §150 (p. 202) it enters as the reciprocal of his no. 73, the [12(5/2)+20(3)]-faced solid of the second kind — the small ditrigonal icosidodecahedron, itself photographed as Fig. 15, Taf. IX: "das reziproke gleichflächige Polyeder Fig. 2 Taf. VIII" has equilateral hexagons with alternately equal angles for faces, the icosahedron as its inner core, and the combined vertices of an icosahedron and a dodecahedron. Then in §153, "Die vollständige Figur der Ebenen des Ikosaeders" (pp. 206–207), he re-derives the same hexagon from the stellation diagram — the points labelled 1 and 2 of the complete figure together bound the face of the solid of Fig. 2 Taf. VIII — crediting the complete-figure method in footnotes to Hess's 1876 treatise. So Brückner already exhibits it in 1900 both as a uniform dual and as a stellation of the icosahedron.

history: This solid — to the eye a regular dodecahedron whose twelve faces have been dug out into pentagonal pyramidal pits, leaving a surface of sixty equilateral triangles — made a double debut in Germany in 1876, and with a dispute built in. Theodor Hügel, in a book printed in Neustadt an der Haardt with 113 stereoscopic figures (Die regulären und halbregulären Polyeder), announced it as nothing less than a fifth regular star polyhedron, his "twenty-cornered wedge icosahedron" bounded by twenty planes; the claim rested on a loose definition of Poinsot's star polyhedra. Max Brückner later took the claim apart: the twenty faces are crossed hexagons winding twice about their centres, and the corners alternate salient and re-entrant angles, so every face is alike and every vertex is alike, but nothing is regular. (Hügel's book was not all blunder — Guy Inchbald's history credits it with the first correct drawing of the regular star hexagon {6/2}, fixing an error of Poinsot's.) That same year Edmund Hess published in Kassel his memoir on polyhedra that are simultaneously isogonal and isohedral — the founding study of what are now called noble polyhedra — and it is inside Hess's theory that this figure found its proper home.

In Vielecke und Vielflache (1900) Brückner photographed his paper model of it (Taf. VIII, Fig. 26) and gave it the fullest treatment it had yet received. He derived its face from the complete figure of the icosahedron's twenty planes — the stellation diagram, in later language — and catalogued it among the non-convex noble polyhedra as the "20-cornered 20-hedron of the tenth kind", declaring it autopolar: self-dual. Its innermost kernel is the icosahedron, its outer hull the dodecahedron, and the pyramids sunk into the dodecahedron's faces count as hollows in his density arithmetic (twenty doubly-wound faces and twenty doubly-wound vertices on sixty edges give 40 + 40 = 60 + 2·10 under Hess's extended Euler formula, hence "tenth kind"). As a star polyhedron it has 20 faces, 60 edges and 20 vertices, Euler characteristic −20.

At the 1924 International Mathematical Congress in Toronto, A. Harry Wheeler — the Massachusetts schoolteacher whose polyhedron models now fill a Smithsonian collection — listed it as form 9 of his icosahedra under the cryptic name "Möbius (Concave)". His paper prints the name in a table without a word of explanation, and no documented link between August Möbius and this solid has surfaced: Brückner's many Möbius citations concern one-sided surfaces and general polyhedron theory, not this figure. In The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938) Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie admitted it as Ef₁g₁ — every cell through shell e, both mirror halves of the 120-cell f₁ orbit, and the thirty g₁ bipyramids, 341 cells in all — and the Crennells' 1999 renumbering made it stellation 26 of the 59. Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) fixed its popular identity as model 28, the "third stellation of the icosahedron", and the now-standard name "excavated dodecahedron" is simply descriptive; who coined it is unknown.

Its mathematical afterlife turns on the properties Hess and Brückner spotted first. It is noble — face-transitive and vertex-transitive at once, one of the few classical noble solids beyond the regular polyhedra — and self-dual: reciprocating it about its midsphere returns the same figure. Self-duality is exactly why it leads a double life. Read on the dodecahedron's twenty vertices, with thirty of its sixty edges the dodecahedron's own and the other thirty the longer edges of a great stellated dodecahedron, it is a faceting of the dodecahedron; and since stellating the icosahedron and faceting the dodecahedron are reciprocal processes (systematized by Bridge in 1974 and by Inchbald, whose tables list this faceting as self-dual and caution that the visible dimple apexes are "false vertices"), the stellation and the faceting are one and the same shape. There is even a late vindication of Hügel's over-eager 1876 claim: Cutler and Schulte (2010) identified the excavated dodecahedron as one of just ten abstract regular polyhedra of index two with vertices in a single orbit — combinatorially it is a regular polyhedron whose geometric realization displays only half of its abstract symmetries. In 2020 Ulrich Mikloweit, sweeping the facetings of the uniform polyhedra with the program Stella4D, duly recovered it among the noble facetings of the dodecahedron: "an icosahedron too, made of crossed 6-gons. It is self-dual."
info.bruckner_context: Brückner photographs his paper model as Taf. VIII, Fig. 26 and returns to the solid three times in the text. In the historical remarks on star polyhedra (Nr. 137, p. 178) he demolishes Hügel's 1876 claim that it is a fifth regular star polyhedron: its twenty faces are crossed ("second-kind") hexagons, not regular polygons, and its six-edged corners alternate salient and re-entrant angles. In Nr. 153 he derives that crossed-hexagon face from the "vollständige Figur" of the icosahedron's twenty planes — the device now called the stellation diagram. And in Nr. 161 (item 4) he catalogues it among the non-convex polyhedra that are at once isogonal and isohedral — noble, in modern terms — as "das 20-eckige 20-Flach der 10. Art", stating explicitly that it is "autopolar" (self-dual), with the icosahedron as innermost kernel, the dodecahedron as outer hull, and the sunken pentagonal pyramids counted as hollows of coefficient zero in his density bookkeeping.

history: Take ten regular tetrahedra and inscribe them all in one regular dodecahedron, so that their forty corners land in coinciding pairs on the dodecahedron's twenty vertices, and you get one of exactly five compounds symmetric enough to be called regular — the same short list that contains the stella octangula and the compound of five cubes. Who found it first is genuinely disputed. The standard modern attribution, repeated across Wikipedia's compound articles, is the German mathematician Edmund Hess in 1876. But Guy Inchbald's history of stellation argues the compound is decades older: in his 1812/13 memoir Recherches sur les polyedres, written in the wake of Poinsot's 1809 rediscovery of the star polyhedra, Augustin-Louis Cauchy — in Inchbald's words — "is also aware of the regular compounds, of five and ten tetrahedra and of five octahedra, as stellations of the regular icosahedron". The two traditions do not even agree on the Hess side of the ledger: Inchbald's own timeline contains no 1876 entry for Hess at all (his Hess entry is 1883), so the fairest summary is that Cauchy appears to have known the compound around 1812, and Hess is usually credited with first describing it systematically in 1876.

The compound then entered the model-building tradition. Max Brückner built and photographed a paper model for Vielecke und Vielflache (Leipzig, 1900), where it appears as Tafel IX, Fig. 3, and M. C. Escher later drew much of his knowledge of stellated polyhedra and compounds from that very book — though the compounds Escher actually put into prints like Stars (1948) were the octahedral and cubic ones; no appearance of the ten-tetrahedra compound in his work is documented. In 1924 Albert Harry Wheeler of Worcester, Massachusetts showed his icosahedron models at the International Mathematical Congress in Toronto and listed this one as his no. 8, "Ten intersecting tetrahedra". When Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie enumerated the stellations of the icosahedron in The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938), it became the stellation Ef₁: everything out through cell-shell e, plus all 120 tetrahedral cells of shell f₁ — 311 of the 473 cells in all. In the Crennell numbering added to the 1999 Tarquin edition it is stellation 22 of 59.

The Du Val symbol tells the compound's best story: chirality. The 120 congruent tetrahedral cells of shell f₁ form a single orbit under the full icosahedral symmetry group, but under rotations alone they split into two mirror-image sets of 60. The inner core E plus one hand is the chiral compound of five tetrahedra (Crennell 47, written with unbolded f₁); the core plus both hands is the ten-tetrahedra compound, which is why Du Val prints its f₁ in bold — and why the compound is fully mirror-symmetric while its two five-fold halves are not. It even skirts Miller's rule (v), which bans stellations that fall apart into two complete-symmetry pieces: the two five-tetrahedra compounds inside it share the entire core E, so it is not a disjoint union and survives into the 59. Equivalently, it is what you get from the compound of five cubes by replacing each cube with a stella octangula.

Its later catalog life is dense. Cundy and Rollett's Mathematical Models (1952) taught generations of model-makers to build "Ten Tetrahedra in a Dodecahedron"; Magnus Wenninger published it as model 25 of Polyhedron Models (1971), between the other two icosahedral regular compounds; and John Skilling's 1976 enumeration of the 75 uniform polyhedral compounds gave it the index UC6. Modern sources also note the tidy inversion of its construction: its convex hull is a regular dodecahedron and the solid common to all ten tetrahedra is a regular icosahedron — the very solid whose stellation it is.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner photographed his paper model of the ten-tetrahedra compound as Tafel IX, Fig. 3 of Vielecke und Vielflache (1900), among his plates of star-forms and icosahedron stellations — the plate reference is confirmed both by the cross-reference table in Wikipedia's article on The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra and by this project's earlier research notes. Guy Inchbald's history credits the book with describing "the known stellations, together with six more stellations of the icosahedron"; the ten-tetrahedra compound was among the already-known figures Brückner modelled and photographed, not one of his six additions.

history: Five regular octahedra sharing one centre, interlocked so that their 40 triangular faces lie two by two in just 20 planes — the face planes of an icosahedron, with each plane carrying a six-pointed star formed by two triangles from two different octahedra. That is why it is a stellation: in Du Val's 1938 notation it is C, the core icosahedron plus the first two shells of cells (51 cells in all), third of the fifty-nine. Its 30 vertices are exactly the 30 vertices of an icosidodecahedron, one octahedron vertex per hull vertex, which makes it the only one of the five regular polyhedral compounds whose convex hull is not a regular solid. Unlike its cousin the compound of five tetrahedra it is not chiral: the symmetries fixing one octahedron form the pyritohedral group of order 24 inside the full icosahedral group of order 120, so the five-fold orbit already contains all the reflections.

Who found it first is genuinely disputed. The standard modern attribution, repeated across Wikipedia's compound articles, is Edmund Hess in 1876, in his monograph 'Über die zugleich gleicheckigen und gleichflächigen Polyeder' (Schriften der Gesellschaft zur Beförderung der gesammten Naturwissenschaften zu Marburg 11, pp. 5–97) — the same work credited with the compounds of five tetrahedra, ten tetrahedra and five cubes. But Guy Inchbald's history of stellation argues that Augustin-Louis Cauchy already knew it six decades earlier: in his 'Recherches sur les polyèdres' (work of 1812, published 1813 in the Journal de l'École Polytechnique), Cauchy, in Inchbald's words, 'is also aware of the regular compounds, of five and ten tetrahedra and of five octahedra, as stellations of the regular icosahedron'. The two accounts have never been reconciled — Inchbald's own timeline has no 1876 entry for Hess at all (his Hess entry is 1883) — so the honest summary is that Cauchy appears to have known the compound around 1812, and Hess gave the first systematic published description in 1876.

The model tradition runs straight through Marburg to Leipzig. Max Brückner, working squarely in Hess's school, built a paper model and photographed it for Vielecke und Vielflache (Leipzig, 1900) as figure 6 of plate IX, and in the text he shows how to read the compound directly off the 'complete figure' of the icosahedron's planes — the ancestor of the stellation diagram — citing Hess's 1876 monograph by page. Albert Harry Wheeler, the Massachusetts schoolteacher who exhibited his stellation models at the 1924 International Mathematical Congress in Toronto, listed it as his number 3, 'five intersecting octahedra'. Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie enshrined it in The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938) as the mainline stellation C, and the Crennells' 1999 numbering for the Tarquin edition made it number 3 of 59. Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) made it model 23, one of the trio of regular-compound models (23–25) that generations of paper modellers have built; Cundy and Rollett's Mathematical Models had already given building instructions in 1952.

Later mathematics tidied up its credentials. In Coxeter's Regular Polytopes notation it is [5{3,4}]2{3,5}: the '2{3,5}' after the bracket records that its faces lie doubled in the twenty icosahedron planes, and the absence of any symbol before the bracket records precisely that its vertices do not form a regular polyhedron — alone among the five regular compounds. In John Skilling's complete 1976 enumeration of the 75 uniform polyhedral compounds (Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 79, pp. 447–457) it is UC17. Its dual is the compound of five cubes, the figure usually drawn inscribed in a dodecahedron — which is emphatically not a stellation of the icosahedron but a stellation of the rhombic triacontahedron, and Brückner photographed that one too, as figure 24 of plate XII. The modern nickname 'small icosicosahedron' comes from the compound-naming tradition: shrink each stella octangula of the ten-tetrahedra compound (the 'icosicosahedron') to the octahedral core shared by its two tetrahedra, and this compound is what remains.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner derives this compound in §153 (p. 206), "Die vollständige Figur der Ebenen des Ikosaeders" — his complete figure of the icosahedron's face planes, the direct ancestor of the modern stellation diagram. He labels the intersection points on one face plane by concentric circles and reads compounds straight off the labels: the points marked 3 yield "five concentric octahedra", photographed as his paper model in Fig. 6 of Taf. IX. Footnotes to §153 credit the method to "Hess III" (S. 18 and S. 36), which Brückner defines as Hess's 1876 monograph on isogonal-isohedral polyhedra; the reciprocal compound of five cubes appears via the triacontahedron's complete figure (§156) as Fig. 24 of Taf. XII.

history: The great dodecahedron is the youngest of the four regular star polyhedra, and the only Kepler–Poinsot solid with ordinary convex faces: twelve pentagons that plunge through one another so that five of them wind twice around every vertex. Its 12 vertices and 30 edges are exactly those of the icosahedron; each face is the pentagon spanned by the five neighbours of a vertex. It was discovered by Louis Poinsot in the memoir "Mémoire sur les polygones et les polyèdres", presented in 1809 and printed in the Journal de l'École Polytechnique in 1810. Where Kepler had starred the faces, Poinsot starred the corners: admitting vertices whose figure is a pentagram, he found two genuinely new regular solids — this one, which he called the nouveau dodécaèdre, and the great icosahedron — while also rediscovering Kepler's two stellated dodecahedra, apparently without knowing Kepler had them. He correctly computed the new dodecahedron's density, 3. A tantalizing prehistory is disputed: Wikipedia states that Wenzel Jamnitzer depicted a great dodecahedron in his Perspectiva Corporum Regularium of 1568, but Max Brückner, examining the same plate in 1900, flatly denied it — the broken edge-lines show "only an icosahedron with inward-set pyramids", the solid's exterior look-alike rather than the self-intersecting solid itself.

Poinsot could not prove his list complete; Augustin Cauchy did, by showing that every regular star polyhedron arises from a Platonic solid by extending its faces or edges — in modern language, the great dodecahedron is the second of the three stellations of the dodecahedron. Even the date carries a small dispute: Brückner says Cauchy had the proof "bereits 1811" (already in 1811), Wikipedia and Inchbald place the work in 1812, and the memoir "Recherches sur les polyèdres" appeared in print in 1813. In 1858 Joseph Bertrand gave a slicker derivation by faceting the icosahedron and dodecahedron, and the next year Arthur Cayley, in two notes in the Philosophical Magazine ("On Poinsot's Four New Regular Solids", vol. 17, 1859, pp. 123–127 and 209), fixed the correct densities Poinsot had missed for Kepler's two solids, observed that the four stars fall into two polar pairs, and coined the English names used ever since — great dodecahedron among them. Cayley admitted in the second note that he had learned of Cauchy's memoir only after the first was published; Brückner later sniffed that the names Cayley introduced were "not happily chosen". Acceptance was never unanimous: Ludwig Schläfli refused to admit the great dodecahedron and its dual as genuine polyhedra because V − E + F = 12 − 30 + 12 = −6 violates Euler's formula.

The solid then passed into the great nineteenth-century German model-building tradition. Brückner reports (citing Siegmund Günther) that Poinsot himself had already made models of his stars; Christian Wiener's Über Vielecke und Vielflache (Leipzig, 1864) gave the first exemplary illustrations drawn from models, together with the nets; Theodor Hügel's 1876 tract came with 113 stereoscopic double images including the regular stars. At Marburg, Edmund Hess — whose German nomenclature Brückner adopted, the great dodecahedron being his "12-flächiges Stern-12-Eck" — pushed the subject furthest, and in 1877 discovered a subtle companion: a noble (isogonal and isohedral), self-dual polyhedron with twelve self-intersecting decagonal faces whose exterior is indistinguishable from the great dodecahedron's. Brückner's Vielecke und Vielflache (1900) is this tradition's monument: his paper model of the great dodecahedron, photographed on Tafel IX as Fig. 7, illustrates both Poinsot's regular solid and Hess's noble look-alike, since a photograph can only show the shared outside. Brückner donated some 200 models to Heidelberg University shortly before his death in 1934; George Hart records that no one knows what became of them.

A claim sometimes attached to this solid — that it was sold as a toy puzzle in the nineteenth century — could not be confirmed in any citable source. The documented facts nearby are these: William Rowan Hamilton's 1857 icosian game, marketed from 1859 by John Jaques as "The Traveller's Dodecahedron, or A Voyage Round the World", was a genuine Victorian polyhedron puzzle, but it was played on an ordinary convex dodecahedron, not the great one. The great dodecahedron got its own mass-market puzzle only in 1982, when the American mathematician Adam Alexander released Alexander's Star, a Rubik's-Cube-style twisty puzzle in the shape of a great dodecahedron. In the twentieth century the solid became a staple of the model literature — it is model 21 of Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971), sitting between its dual, the small stellated dodecahedron (W20), and the great stellated dodecahedron (W22) in the dodecahedron's stellation series.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner shows the great dodecahedron twice: as an engraved line drawing, Fig. 22 Taf. VII, and as a photographed paper model, Fig. 7 Taf. IX. In §128 he derives it from the icosahedron — the twelve planes each spanned by the five neighbours of a vertex — names it "das 12-flächige Stern-12-Eck der 3. Art" (12-faced star-12-vertex solid of density 3, by Hess's first formula), and notes its innermost kernel is a dodecahedron. His historical §137 covers Poinsot, Cauchy, Bertrand and Cayley, rejects Günther's claim that Jamnitzer drew the solid in 1568, and grumbles that Cayley's English names are "nicht glücklich gewählt" (not happily chosen). Remarkably, the same photograph does double duty: in §161 no. 3 he cites Fig. 7 Taf. IX again for Hess's noble, self-dual "12-eckiges 12-Flach der 18. Art" (Hess, Marburger Berichte 1877), a 12-faced, 12-vertex polyhedron with self-intersecting decagonal faces that is, per his own footnote, "nach seinem äusseren Ansehen identisch" — outwardly identical — with the great dodecahedron, so one model photograph serves both polyhedra.

history: Five regular tetrahedra share a common center, arranged so that their twenty corners are exactly the twenty vertices of a regular dodecahedron. It is one of the five regular polyhedral compounds, and the strange one of the family: its only symmetries are the sixty rotations of the icosahedron — no mirror belongs to it — so it exists as two enantiomorphs, a right-handed and a left-handed compound, and superimposing them produces the mirror-symmetric compound of ten tetrahedra. Read through The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra, it is the stellation Ef₁, Crennell's number 47: the 120 tetrahedral cells of Du Val's shell f₁ are the only orbit in the whole 473-cell arrangement that splits into two mirror sets of sixty when reflections are dropped, and gluing one sixty-cell hand onto the core E yields one hand of the compound (251 cells in all). Strangest of its habits: reciprocate it about its midsphere and you get not the same figure but its own mirror image — in Wikipedia's words, if the faces are twisted to the right, then the vertices are twisted to the left. Very few polyhedra behave this way; its dual is its enantiomorph.

Who found it first is genuinely disputed. Wikipedia and most modern references state flatly that it was first described by Edmund Hess in 1876. But Guy Inchbald's history of stellation reads Augustin-Louis Cauchy's memoir Recherches sur les polyedres — presented in 1812, printed 1813 in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique — as already aware of the regular compounds of five and ten tetrahedra and of five octahedra 'as stellations of the regular icosahedron', six decades before Hess. The two accounts cannot even be matched publication-for-publication: Inchbald's own timeline has no 1876 Hess entry at all (his Hess entry is 1883), so the safest formula is that Hess gave the first systematic description in 1876 while Cauchy appears to have known the figure in 1812/13. From there it threads through every later catalog: Max Brückner photographed his paper model of it in 1900; Albert Harry Wheeler, a high-school teacher from Worcester, Massachusetts, presenting his icosahedral forms at the 1924 International Mathematical Congress in Toronto, was the only cataloguer ever to number the two hands separately — 7 for the right, 6 for the left — under the name 'Five intersecting Tetrahedra'; Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie fixed it among the 59 in 1938; the Crennell numbering added for the 1999 Tarquin edition placed it at 47, inside the chiral block (33–59) that lists only right-handed forms; and John Skilling's 1976 complete enumeration of uniform compounds made it UC5. Coxeter's symbol {5,3}[5{3,3}]{3,5} compresses the whole geometry into one line: five tetrahedra sharing the dodecahedron's vertices on the left and the icosahedron's face planes on the right.

This solid is also the documented link between Brückner's book and M. C. Escher. Escher studied Vielecke und Vielflache in detail — the likely conduit was his half-brother Berend, a geology professor versed in crystallography — and the proof is an undated colored-pencil sketch of the compound of five tetrahedra bearing Escher's handwritten note that he learned of it in 'Table IX, n. 11' of Brückner. George Hart, who reproduced the sketch in his 2019 Bridges paper on Brückner, observes that Escher kept the handedness of Brückner's photograph but drew the compound from a different viewpoint, centered on a vertex, with one color per tetrahedron: he had not traced the plate, he had understood the object, and he built his own cardboard model, which still survives. The Escher catalogue of Bool and others (1982) records the model as a study for his woodcuts, and in 1958 Escher carved the structure in maple as a fifteen-centimeter sculpture, evolving the five tetrahedra into a symmetric arrangement of flowers.

Among model-builders it may be the best-loved object in the whole polyhedral canon. Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) presents it as model 24, assembled — in MathWorld's account of his method — from twenty identical three-part vertex pyramids joined in rings of five; it is kind to builders because it is fully supported, with no overhanging faces, yet chiral, a combination that Robert Webb's Stella documentation counts in only two of the 59 stellations. In 1995 the mathematician Thomas Hull re-imagined it as 'Five Intersecting Tetrahedra' (FIT), a modular origami wireframe of five interwoven tetrahedral frames that effectively founded the genre Robert Lang later named polypolyhedra; Michal Kosmulski's origami pages call it 'probably the most popular model of the woven polyhedron type'. Hull's title, coined for paper-folders in 1995, had been anticipated by Wheeler's 1924 catalog name 'Five intersecting Tetrahedra' by seventy-one years.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner shows the compound as a hand-built paper model, photographed as figure 11 on Tafel IX of Vielecke und Vielflache (1900) — one of the 146 models arrayed on shelves across the book's ten photographic plates. Plate IX gathers its relatives around it: n. 3 is the compound of ten tetrahedra and n. 6 the compound of five octahedra (identifications from George Hart's Bridges 2019 caption), so the chiral five-tetrahedra compound sits beside the mirror-complete compounds it half-composes. Guy Inchbald's stellation history credits the 1900 book with describing "the known stellations, together with six more stellations of the icosahedron". This exact plate-and-figure citation, "Table IX, n. 11", is what Escher wrote on his sketch of the compound — making this photograph the one documented bridge between Brückner's book and Escher's polyhedral art.

history: The shape enters the printed record in Nuremberg in 1568, half a century before anyone understood what it was. Wenzel Jamnitzer (c. 1508–1585), the city's most celebrated goldsmith, published Perspectiva Corporum Regularium, a book of perspective fantasies on the five Platonic solids with plates by Jost Amman, and modern historians recognize among them a great stellated dodecahedron (and a great dodecahedron). Jamnitzer drew it as ornament, not mathematics: the book's whole plan treats only the five Platonic solids as regular, and Guy Inchbald observes that its long subtitle makes plain Jamnitzer never realized his stars belonged to the same class. Even the identification has been argued over. Max Brückner, re-examining the figures as reproduced in Siegmund Günther's 1876 history of star polygons and polyhedra, objected that one had six-edged corners and another looked like a mere icosahedron with pyramids set on it, and ruled that all pre-Kepler drawings, however similar, were accidental. He also passes on Günther's lovely observation that the morning-star finials then still common on gables and roofs of southern German towns are often built exactly on the pattern of this solid, while a mosaic panel in St Mark's, Venice, shows its small sibling.

The mathematics begins with Johannes Kepler. In Book II of Harmonices Mundi (Linz, 1619) he stated for the first time the general idea of stellation — extend a figure's edges or faces until they close up again — applied it to the pentagon to get the pentagram, and then carried it into three dimensions. Extending the edges of an icosahedron gave him this solid; extending a dodecahedron's gave the small stellated dodecahedron. The discovery, though, was not the shape but the insight: Kepler saw that the faces are regular star pentagons, identically arranged at every vertex, so the ancient list of five regular solids was incomplete. His route left an irony. Because he reached it by working outward from an icosahedron, popular accounts still file the great stellated dodecahedron under that solid — but its twelve pentagram faces lie in the twelve face planes of a dodecahedron, so in the modern face-plane sense it is the third and final stellation of the dodecahedron and no stellation of the icosahedron at all. That is why it is absent from the fifty-nine icosahedra of Coxeter's 1938 book (Miller's rule i excludes it), and Inchbald notes that Coxeter's own introduction misreads Kepler on precisely this point.

Kepler's stars were then largely forgotten for nearly two centuries. Louis Poinsot, at the time a schoolmaster at the Lycée Bonaparte in Paris, rediscovered them in a memoir read in 1809 and printed in the Journal de l'École Polytechnique in 1810 — apparently without knowing Kepler's work, though historians from Günther and Brückner onward have treated that as a judgement rather than a proven fact. Poinsot worked by face-stellating the dodecahedron rather than edge-stellating the icosahedron, and went on to find the two genuinely new solids, the great dodecahedron and great icosahedron. This one he called the dodécaèdre étoilé de quatrième espèce, the starred dodecahedron of the fourth species — wrongly, as Brückner points out: its true density is 7, and Poinsot's 4 came from mismeasuring the area of a pentagram. Augustin-Louis Cauchy, a twenty-one-year-old military engineer on Napoleon's invasion harbour at Cherbourg, then proved (memoir read February 1811, printed 1813) that every regular star polyhedron must arise by extending the edges or faces of a Platonic solid, so Poinsot's four close the list; Joseph Bertrand reproved it more elegantly in 1858 by faceting. The modern names are due to Arthur Cayley, then a London conveyancing barrister, in "On Poinsot's Four New Regular Solids" (Philosophical Magazine, 1859). He coined "great stellated dodecahedron" after Poinsot's construction, giving Kepler's no weight — in 1859 these were Poinsot's solids, and the joint credit in "Kepler–Poinsot" is a later, twentieth-century restoration.

Among the four, this solid and its dual the great icosahedron are the well-behaved pair: V − E + F = 20 − 30 + 12 = 2, so when Ludwig Schläfli around 1860 refused the name polyhedron to the two stars that violate Euler's formula, the great stellated dodecahedron passed his test untouched. Its twenty vertices are exactly a dodecahedron's — it is the only Kepler–Poinsot solid whose convex hull is a dodecahedron rather than an icosahedron — and it shares with its dual the deepest density of any regular polyhedron, 7. Brückner photographed his paper model of it in 1900 among the 146 models of Vielecke und Vielflache; Magnus Wenninger made it model 22 of Polyhedron Models, and it remains one of the most-built star polyhedra, its silhouette having served as ornament for centuries, from Amman's etching to the gable stars Günther catalogued.

history: The fourth stellation is the plainest kind of citizen among the icosahedron's famous stellations: Du Val's D, the solid you get by taking every cell of the first four shells — the core icosahedron, 20 shallow face-pyramids, 30 triangular bipyramids and 60 quadrilateral pyramids, 111 cells in all. It is the fourth of the eight "mainline" stellations A through H. Its paper trail starts with Edmund Hess of Marburg, who is credited with discovering the mainline stellated icosahedra beyond Poinsot's great icosahedron by working from stellation diagrams; Wikipedia dates this to his 1876 monograph Über die zugleich gleicheckigen und gleichflächigen Polyeder, while the Polytope Wiki's entry for this solid says 1875 and Guy Inchbald's history timeline instead places Hess's stellation-and-facetting work at 1883 — the sources genuinely disagree, and nobody seems to have checked Hess's own pages for this particular figure.

Max Brückner made it visible. Plate IX of Vielecke und Vielflache (1900) — one of the five collotype double-plates photographed by the Dresden art-printing house Römmler & Jonas — shows his paper model of D as Fig. 17, shelved among the regular compounds that made the plate famous. Brückner derived the icosahedron's stellations from the complete face-plane figure in §153, scrupulously footnoting the method to Hess; his book contains ten icosahedron stellations, and George Hart's 2019 study of the book notes he was the first to construct several of them, though no source singles out D as one of his firsts. Brückner's original models are lost, which makes the photograph the oldest surviving image of the solid.

The American connection comes in 1924, when A. Harry Wheeler — a Worcester, Massachusetts high-school teacher and compulsive model-builder — presented his list of icosahedron "forms" as an invited speaker at the Toronto International Congress of Mathematicians. This solid is his no. 4, which he called the "nonagonal" form, naming it (as he named his no. 2 the "hexagonal") after its face figure: read as a single star polyhedron, D has twenty nine-sided faces. Wheeler pointedly avoided the word "stellation" altogether. Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie folded it into The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938) as mainline D, and the Crennells' 1999 third edition made it number 4 of the 59. Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) skipped it, so it has no Wenninger number — and confusingly, the model Wenninger does call the "fourth stellation" (W29) is an entirely different solid, Crennell 11, the set of thirty disconnected bipyramids.

Its modern rehabilitation is the best part of the story. The Polytope Wiki calls it the noble enneagrammic icosahedron: a noble polyhedron — face-transitive and vertex-transitive at once, a rare distinction outside the regular and uniform families — with 20 triangular-symmetric enneagram (nine-sided star) faces, 90 edges and 60 vertices, density 5, its 60 vertices lying at the vertices of a small rhombicosidodecahedron. Better still, it is the conjugate of the final stellation of the icosahedron: the echidnahedron's faces are irregular 9/4 enneagrams, and swapping them for the shallower-winding enneagrams of the same abstract polygon turns the spikiest of the 59 into this modest one. The unassuming fourth stellation and the celebrated final stellation are, abstractly, the same polyhedron worn two different ways — a pairing between Crennell 4 and Crennell 8 that nobody in 1900 could have stated.
info.bruckner_context: Taf. IX, Fig. 17 is Brückner's collotype photograph of his own paper model of stellation D, sitting on the same double-plate as his icosahedral showpieces — the compounds of ten tetrahedra (Fig. 3), five octahedra (Fig. 6) and five tetrahedra (Fig. 11) — plus one more icosahedron stellation at Fig. 20 (George Hart's 2019 caption identifies Figs. 17 and 20 as the plate's two icosahedron stellations). In §153 of Vielecke und Vielflache Brückner intersects each icosahedron face plane with the nineteen others, building what is in effect the stellation diagram, and derives such figures from it — crediting the method, in footnotes, to Hess's 1876 monograph. A footnote on p. 183 states generally that a large part of the polyhedra on the collotype plates were modelled by him for the first time; whether that claim covers Fig. 17 specifically he does not say.

history: This is the one solid on plate IX that Brückner explicitly claims as his own discovery. In section 153 of Vielecke und Vielflache (Teubner, Leipzig, 1900, pp. 206–207) he reads the famous stellations out of the "complete figure" of the icosahedron's face planes one by one, carefully footnoting Edmund Hess for the older ones — and then announces a polyhedron "bisher noch nicht beschrieben", never yet described. It is isohedral, of higher kind: twenty nine-sided faces, each a (6+3)-gon of the fourth kind with six angles of one size and three of another, ninety edges, and thirty-two vertices in two rings — twelve sharp five-sided spikes standing over the vertices of an icosahedron and twenty blunter six-edged points over the vertices of a dodecahedron. By Hess's density formula he reckons the whole solid to be of the 11th kind. Figure 20 of Tafel IX is the photograph of his own paper model; no earlier maker or author is cited because, as far as anyone has ever shown, there was none.

The solid's second life began at the 1924 International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto, where Albert Harry Wheeler (1873–1950), a high-school mathematics teacher from Worcester, Massachusetts and an invited speaker, presented his method of assembling stellated forms from the cells of the stellation diagram. His icosahedral series lists this solid as number 18 under the curious name "Double 13 + 10" — and the name decodes exactly. His no. 13 is the solid Coxeter's school would later write De₂f₂, whose exterior is twelve five-sided trapezohedral crowns; his no. 10 is De₁, the "twenty-pointed, six-edged" form. Merge the two cell sets and you get D + e₁ + e₂ + f₂ = Ef₂, this solid precisely: Wheeler's name simply says his figures 13 and 10, doubled into one. (The union arithmetic is ours, from Du Val's symbols; the name itself is Wheeler's as recorded in the standard concordance.) Wheeler's hundreds of paper models, made in Worcester and given to the Smithsonian by Helen M. Wheeler, still exist — the museum's digitized collection includes several of his stellated icosahedra, among them his model of the twelve-spiked no. 13 ingredient, though a surviving model of no. 18 itself could not be confirmed.

In The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938), Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie admitted it — it passes Miller's rules — with the cell symbol Ef₂: everything through shell e plus the twelve f₂ trapezohedra, 203 of the 473 cells. The twelve trapezohedra tips reach the same radius as the great icosahedron's vertices, which is exactly why Brückner could say its pentagonal spikes stand at the vertices of an icosahedron. H. T. Flather made card models of all fifty-nine, preserved in the mathematics library at Cambridge, so a physical Ef₂ has existed continuously since the 1930s; in the Crennells' 1999 third edition it became number 28. Modern literature upholds Brückner's priority mostly by silence rather than statement: Wikipedia's table cites Taf. IX Fig. 20 against Crennell 28 without any discovery narrative, and Guy Inchbald's history of stellation says only that Brückner described "the known stellations, together with six more stellations of the icosahedron", without naming the six. This solid — flagged as new in Brückner's own words while its section-mates carry Hess citations — is evidently one of them, and no source disputes him.

Its later fame is modest, which makes Brückner's photograph the more precious. It never acquired a common name; Magnus Wenninger left it out of the seventeen icosahedron stellations he modelled in Polyhedron Models (1971), so it has no Wenninger number; it survives in the catalogues — MathWorld's stellation table, George Hart's virtual-polyhedra pages as entry "28. Ef2" with wireframe and five-colour models — as one of the quieter members of the fifty-nine, a solid essentially nobody has celebrated since the man who first noticed, in 1900, that nobody had ever described it.
info.bruckner_context: Section 153, "Die vollständige Figur der Ebenen des Ikosaeders" (pp. 206–207), walks outward through the complete figure of one icosahedron face plane cut by the other nineteen (Fig. 17, Taf. II), reading off the five-octahedra, five- and ten-tetrahedra compounds, the great icosahedron, the first stellation and the excavated dodecahedron — with footnotes to Hess for the previously known ones. Then, with no citation to anyone, Brückner derives one more: join each of the three points 7 to the two points 6 on the opposite side of the triangle 7,7,7, add the segments between points 6 parallel to its edges, and the result is a nine-gon — a (6+3)-gon of the fourth kind with six angles of one size and three of another. Twenty of these bound the isohedral polyhedron photographed as Fig. 20 of Tafel IX, which he announces as "ein bisher noch nicht beschriebenes gleichflächiges Polyeder höherer Art" (a hitherto never-described isohedral polyhedron of higher kind), reckons to be of the 11th kind by Hess's formula, and describes precisely: twelve regular five-edged vertices at the vertices of an icosahedron, twenty hexagonal vertices at the vertices of a dodecahedron.

history: Most of the celebrated stellations of the icosahedron were famous before anyone called them stellations: the great icosahedron goes back to Poinsot in 1809, the regular compounds to Cauchy or Hess. The sixth stellation has no such pedigree — its first known appearance anywhere is a photograph. Max Brückner, the Bautzen schoolmaster who spent decades building polyhedral models, shows it at plate X, figure 3 of Vielecke und Vielflache (Teubner, Leipzig, 1900), one of ten stellations of the icosahedron recorded across his collotype plates; a footnote in the book states that a large part of the photographed polyhedra were modelled there for the first time by him. When Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie catalogued the fifty-nine icosahedra in 1938, their cross-reference for this solid pointed back to that plate, and no earlier description has been identified. Wikipedia's history of the subject is blunt: before Coxeter, only Brückner and Wheeler had recorded any significant sets of stellations.

The solid resurfaced in 1924, when A. Harry Wheeler, the Worcester, Massachusetts mathematics teacher whose paper models are now preserved at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, presented his icosahedral forms as an invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto. Wheeler pointedly avoided the word stellation, speaking instead of 'forms' of the icosahedron, and his list of twenty was never meant as a complete enumeration. This one is his number 17, under the cryptic name 'Double 13 + 9' — which turns out to be a recipe: superpose his form 13 (the shape Wenninger would later call the ninth stellation, Du Val De₂f₂) on his form 9 (the excavated dodecahedron, his 'Mobius concave') and the union of their cells is exactly this polyhedron. The cell arithmetic checks perfectly, though no published source spells out the convention.

The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra (1938) gave it its permanent identity: Du Val's symbol Fg₁, meaning everything out through shell f — the 323 cells of the mainline second stellation — plus the thirty triangular bipyramids of the g₁ orbit in the shell beyond, 353 cells in all. It keeps the full icosahedral symmetry, twelve tall spikes and all. H. T. Flather built the complete set of fifty-nine as card models, this one among them; his set survives in the mathematics library of Cambridge University. When Kate and David Crennell reset the book for Tarquin's 1999 third edition and numbered the icosahedra for the first time, it became number 23 of 59 — the numbering everyone now cites.

Its everyday name, though, comes from the model-building tradition. Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (Cambridge University Press, 1971), the book that taught a generation to build polyhedra, includes seventeen icosahedral stellations among its 119 models; this one is model W31, and Wikipedia records that the index numbers and ordinal names — 'sixth stellation of the icosahedron' among them — were allocated arbitrarily by Wenninger's publisher according to their occurrence in the book, with no mathematical significance. The name stuck anyway. In 1985 Tarquin Publications — the same house that would later publish the Crennell edition of The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra — gave the solid a cut-out book of its own, Gerald Jenkins and Magdalen Bear's The Sixth Stellation of the Icosahedron, reissued in 2004 as Advanced Polyhedra 2; the publisher's copy promises 'twelve sharp spikes emerging from pentagonal cups', in ten pairs of parallel face planes, the finished model balancing on exactly three of its spikes. Between Wenninger's instructions and Tarquin's press-out sheets, the solid in Brückner's photograph became a staple of the paper-modelling repertoire, with nets still circulating on hobbyist sites today.

history: The oldest known image of this solid is not in a book but in a floor. Set into the marble pavement of St Mark's Basilica in Venice, just inside the main west door, is a small tarsia panel showing a spiky twelve-pointed star drawn in perspective, ringed by an illusionistic necklace of beads. It is traditionally attributed to Paolo Uccello, the Florentine perspective obsessive who is documented in Venice from 1425 to about 1430 as a master mosaicist — though his one provable Venetian work, a St Peter mosaic of 1425 for the basilica's facade, was destroyed in the seventeenth century. The attribution rests on style, not documents: it was proposed by the art historian Michelangelo Muraro only in 1955, the standard Italian biographical dictionary hedges it as merely probable, and George Hart notes that no one has published the actual evidence for either the attribution or the date. The dates quoted in the mathematical literature drift accordingly, from an impossible 1420 (Uccello had not yet arrived in Venice) to circa 1430. If the panel really is fifteenth-century work, an anonymous marble-cutter beat the mathematicians to this polyhedron by two hundred years.

The mathematics begins with Johannes Kepler, in Book II of Harmonices Mundi (Linz, 1619) — the same book whose fifth part contains his third law of planetary motion. There Kepler states the idea of stellation for the first time: extend the edges or faces of a figure until they meet again, as the pentagon's sides extended become the pentagram. Edge-stellating the dodecahedron gave him this solid, which he nicknamed the echinus, the urchin or hedgehog. His decisive act was not drawing the shape, which craftsmen had done before him, but recognising that it is regular: twelve identical star pentagons, five meeting at every vertex, meaning Euclid's list of five regular solids was incomplete. He worked all this out in the same years he was writing legal briefs defending his mother against a witchcraft prosecution.

Kepler's construction was then forgotten. Louis Poinsot, a Paris schoolmaster at the Lycee Bonaparte, rediscovered the solid in a memoir read in 1809 (printed 1810 in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique), and by also allowing star-shaped vertex figures he added two solids Kepler never had, the great dodecahedron and great icosahedron. Poinsot also noticed something disturbing: for this solid V − E + F = 12 − 30 + 12 = −6, and Euler's formula fails. Augustin-Louis Cauchy — a twenty-one-year-old military engineer on Napoleon's invasion harbour works at Cherbourg — read a memoir to the Institut in February 1811 (published 1813) proving that every regular star polyhedron must come from stellating a convex regular solid, so the regular polyhedra stop at nine; in the process the small stellated dodecahedron took its permanent catalog identity as the first of the dodecahedron's three stellations. The English name arrived in 1859, when Arthur Cayley — then still earning his living as a conveyancing barrister — named all four solids in the Philosophical Magazine; in that paper they were 'Poinsot's four new regular solids', and the joint credit 'Kepler–Poinsot' is a later restoration whose coiner is surprisingly hard to pin down.

The broken Euler count kept the solid controversial: Ludwig Schläfli flatly refused to admit it as a polyhedron (Imre Lakatos later made it the star counterexample of Proofs and Refutations, coining 'monster-barring' for exactly Schläfli's move), until Felix Klein showed in 1877 that the anomaly is really the geometry of a genus-4 Riemann surface, Bring's curve. Meanwhile the solid led a parallel life as an ornament — the iron fence of the Grande Synagogue de Paris (1867–74) is studded with small stellated dodecahedra, chosen because from certain angles their silhouette is a Star of David. Max Brückner photographed his paper model of it in Vielecke und Vielflache (1900), and through that book it reached M. C. Escher, who made it the whole subject of two prints: Order and Chaos (1950), where it pierces a soap bubble amid debris, and Gravitation (June 1952), where each of its twelve pyramidal hollows houses a shell-less tortoise. Escher built his own cardboard model as a study.

history: The solid's paper trail begins, as far as anyone has traced it, on page 191 of Max Brückner's Vielecke und Vielflache (Teubner, Leipzig, 1900) — and Brückner did not call it a stellation of anything. In section 143 of his catalogue of polyhedra of "higher species" it appears as the polar, face-transitive partner of a vertex-transitive star polyhedron: a solid bounded by 24 congruent trapezium faces, its twenty vertices those of a cube plus a cuboctahedron, built in paper and photographed as figures 8 and 13 of plate X. George Hart, surveying the plates in 2019, flatly captions Taf. X no. 13 "the first stellation of the rhombic dodecahedron"; Branko Grünbaum, more fussily, noted in 2008 that Brückner's 24-quadrangle isohedron is not the stellation but merely "isomeghetic" with it — a different polyhedron wearing the same outer shell. Both are right about the silhouette; what the object is depends on how you read its faces, and by Grünbaum's count one silhouette hides at least three polyhedra: the stellation proper (12 self-intersecting hexagons, 36 edges, 20 vertices), the honest solid (48 isosceles triangles, 72 edges, 26 vertices), and a compound of three flattened octahedra (24 overlapping triangles). No description earlier than 1900 turned up in any source consulted here.

The stellation reading, and the modern name, came half a century later. In October 1957 Dorman Luke — the same Luke remembered for the "Dorman Luke construction" for dual polyhedra — published "Stellations of the rhombic dodecahedron" in The Mathematical Gazette (vol. 41, no. 337, pp. 189–194), working from the rhombic dodecahedron's stellation diagram with this solid first on the list; an editorial comment in the Gazette remarked that the first stellation was "of course well known", which is as close as the literature comes to admitting it had been circulating without a birth certificate. The enumeration has been argued over since: Guy Inchbald observes that Luke quietly relaxed Miller's rule (v) and that a postscript signed H.M.C. (Martyn Cundy) wrongly claimed Luke's list obeys the same rules as The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra, and Grünbaum adds that the Gazette's suggestion that the second stellation also appears in Brückner rests on a misunderstanding. Modern counts (Robert Webb's software, reported by MathWorld) give the rhombic dodecahedron three non-trivial stellations — four fully supported counting the core, five under Miller's rules, all mirror-symmetric. Cundy and Rollett's Mathematical Models (2nd edn 1961, p. 127) fixed the first stellation in the model-maker's canon.

M. C. Escher lifted the shape straight from Brückner's plates. His half-brother Berend, a professor of geology with crystallographic interests, is Hart's "likely source" for the book, and Escher's surviving coloured-pencil sketches of two other Brückner compounds carry handwritten notes naming the exact table and figure numbers. In August 1948 he finished the woodcut Study for Stars, whose largest floating form is this solid drawn as an open framework — drawn, tellingly, with edges of the 48-triangle solid rather than of the 12-faced stellation, so it reads equally as three octahedra squashed along their four-fold axes (to 1/√2 of regular height, making the faces isosceles with legs to base as √3 : 2). For the finished wood engraving Stars (October 1948) he swapped it for the compound of three regular octahedra — Brückner's Taf. VIII no. 12, the same construction unflattened — as the chameleon cage; a real artistic decision between two nearly identical star-shapes, reasons unrecorded. The flattened one got its consolation prize thirteen years later: in the lithograph Waterfall (October 1961) it crowns the right-hand tower of the impossible watercourse, with the compound of three cubes (Brückner Taf. IX no. 23) on the left — both towers topped from the 1900 plates. Since stellation, solid and compound share one outer surface, Wikipedia notes that no one can say which of the three Escher meant to depict.

What gives the solid its second life is that it packs: copies fill space with no gaps, in what is now called the stellated rhombic dodecahedral honeycomb — cell-, edge- and vertex-transitive, six cells around every vertex. The packing is the third step of a doubling cascade (Ioana Mihăilă, Bridges 2005): cut every second cube of a checkerboarded cubic packing into six pyramids and glue them onto the neighbours to get rhombic dodecahedra; do the same to the dodecahedra to get Escher's solids; do it once more and you are back to cubes of twice the edge, each tile exactly doubling the volume of the last. Alan Holden's Shapes, Space and Symmetry (1971) had already illustrated how the solids fit together. The doubling is also why the Yoshimoto Cube works: in 1971 the Japanese designer Naoki Yoshimoto, looking for ways to cut a cube exactly in half, found that it splits into two hinged pieces each of which folds into this star; he showed it in 1972 in his exhibition From Cube to Space, and the Museum of Modern Art took it into its permanent collection in 1982. The name "Escher's solid", meanwhile, is younger than it feels: Hart's authoritative 1996 web survey of Escher's polyhedra never uses it, the earliest traced use is Weisstein's encyclopedia entry around 1999, and nobody has ever claimed the coinage.

history: The solid at the top centre of Brückner's Plate XI is the stellation that takes everything: all 473 cells that the icosahedron's twenty face planes carve out of space, sixty long spikes pointing in every direction, and nothing left beyond — which is why it is called final. When Max Brückner published Vielecke und Vielflache in 1900 he was not a professor but the Oberlehrer, the senior master, at the Gymnasium in Bautzen, Saxony, and the book's real sensation was its collotype photographs of 146 paper models, most built by his own hands. By the standard account he was both the first to describe this polyhedron and the first to build it. He reached it through what he called the complete figure of the icosahedron's planes (§153, p. 206) — the direct ancestor of the modern stellation diagram — and in §155 (p. 208) he read the solid's boundary face off that figure's nine outermost points; the photographed model is Tafel XI, Fig. 14. George Hart's study of the book confirms that of its ten icosahedron stellations several, this one included, were Brückner's own firsts.

The method, though, was not his. Brückner's footnotes credit Edmund Hess's 1876 Kassel monograph on isogonal-isohedral polyhedra, and Hess had used such face-plane diagrams to find most of the mainline stellations of the icosahedron a quarter-century earlier; the chain of custody runs Poinsot (1809, the great icosahedron) through Hess (1876) and Brückner (1900) to Wheeler (1924) and Coxeter's circle (1938). Unlike the compounds of five octahedra and five tetrahedra, where sources genuinely disagree about Cauchy-versus-Hess priority, there is no dispute here: every account that names a first for the complete stellation names Brückner. But it is fair to say he climbed a staircase Hess had built — and stood on its top step.

A. H. Wheeler, the American schoolteacher and model-maker, listed the solid in his 1924 Toronto congress paper as his form 12, which he called complete — pointedly avoiding the word stellation altogether. The canonical treatment came in 1938, when Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie's The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra made it the eighth stellation, with Du Val's symbol H: the terminus of the mainline series A through H, meaning every cell out to and including the outermost shell h. Final is meant literally — every triple of the twenty planes meets at or inside the solid, so the stellation process has nowhere further to go. Wheeler was originally to be a co-author of the 1938 book but withdrew, reportedly finding Coxeter's approach cumbersome; H. T. Flather built the models. In the 1999 Tarquin edition Kate and David Crennell numbered the fifty-nine, making it Crennell 8, and it appears there on Plate III.

Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) fixed the modern name: his seventeen icosahedron stellations run from model 26 to model 42, and W42, the last of them, is simply the final stellation — a trophy piece for paper modellers ever since. The newest name arrived by Usenet. On 30 August 1995 Andrew Hume, developer of the Netlib polyhedron database, announced in the geometry.research newsgroup a set of odd solids including "the echidnahedron (my name; its actually the final stellation of the icosahedron)" — after the echidna, the spiny anteater, an apt patron for a solid whose sixty spike tips stand more than eight times as far out as the core icosahedron's vertices. Outwardly it has 92 vertices on three concentric spheres — 12 on the five-fold axes forming an icosahedron, 20 on the three-fold axes forming a dodecahedron, and the 60 tips forming a nonuniform truncated icosahedron — with 180 visible triangular facelets and 270 edges; read instead as a self-intersecting star polyhedron it has just 20 faces, one irregular nine-pointed star in each face plane, 90 edges and 60 vertices. MathWorld adopted Hume's name, records closed forms for the surface area and volume, and attributes the coinage only vaguely to the Netlib database — the Usenet posting pins it down.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner devotes §§153–155 of Vielecke und Vielflache to reading solids off the vollständige Figur der Ebenen des Ikosaeders — the complete figure of the icosahedron's face planes (§153, p. 206), his ancestor of the modern stellation diagram, credited by footnote to Hess's 1876 Kassel monograph. The final stellation is the climax of that run: in §155 (p. 208) he derives its boundary face by joining the figure's nine outermost points, those labelled 8 (the project's reading of the scan counts twenty-seven double points on the resulting face), and his whitewashed paper model is photographed at the top centre of Plate XI as Fig. 14. A footnote on p. 183 states that a large part of the polyhedra on the plates were modelled for the first time by him, and Hart's 2019 study identifies this figure as the final stellation and as one of Brückner's own firsts.

history: The great icosahedron is the youngest of the four regular star polyhedra, and the only one with no known anticipation before the nineteenth century. Its three siblings all have Renaissance shadows: a marble mosaic of the small stellated dodecahedron in St Mark's Basilica in Venice, sometimes attributed to Paolo Uccello (c. 1430), and woodcuts of the great stellated dodecahedron and the great dodecahedron in Wenzel Jamnitzer's Perspectiva corporum regularium (Nuremberg, 1568) — though Jamnitzer plainly did not realise his figures were regular. For the great icosahedron the record is empty. Nobody seems to have drawn it, carved it, or imagined it before Louis Poinsot, a French mechanician, produced it in his 1809 memoir on polygons and polyhedra (published in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique, vol. 4, 1810, pp. 16-49). Working with 'polyhedra of a higher kind' — figures that wind around their centre more than once — Poinsot rediscovered Kepler's two stellated dodecahedra, apparently independently, and added two genuinely new regular solids: the great dodecahedron and the great icosahedron, the latter with twenty triangular faces, twelve vertices arranged in pentagrams, and density 7 (it wraps its centre seven times).

The question Poinsot left open — are there more? — was settled almost immediately by the young Augustin-Louis Cauchy. In his 1813 memoir 'Recherches sur les polyedres' (work of 1812, published in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique, tome 9, cahier 16, pp. 68-86), Cauchy applied symmetry arguments to show that any regular star polyhedron must share its face planes with a Platonic solid — that is, it must be what we now call a stellation — and by stellating the regular solids he proved Poinsot's list of four is complete. In the process the great icosahedron was identified as a stellation of the ordinary icosahedron, the fact that puts it on this page. Cauchy himself avoided the word 'stellated', sticking with Poinsot's 'higher kind' language. Joseph Bertrand gave a more elegant completeness proof in 1858 by faceting rather than stellating, and in 1859 Arthur Cayley, verifying the figures' regularity by coordinate geometry ('On Poinsot's Four New Regular Solids', Philosophical Magazine, ser. 4, vol. 17, pp. 123-127), coined the English names still in use — 'great icosahedron' among them, translating Poinsot's 'etoile' as 'stellated' where needed.

Among the fifty-nine icosahedra of Coxeter, Du Val, Flather and Petrie (1938), the great icosahedron holds a singular position: it is the only Kepler-Poinsot solid in the list. The great stellated dodecahedron is excluded because Kepler obtained it by extending the icosahedron's edges, which creates new face planes rather than reusing the twenty; the small stellated dodecahedron and great dodecahedron are stellations of the dodecahedron, not the icosahedron. In Du Val's notation the great icosahedron is G, a 'mainline' stellation containing every cell out through shell g — 413 of the 473 cells in the whole arrangement. Each of its twelve great spikes is one pentagonal trapezohedron (an f2 cell) capped by five quadrilateral pyramids (g2 cells); its vertices stand phi-cubed (about 4.24) times as far out as the core icosahedron's, and its edges are phi-to-the-fourth (about 6.85) times the core edge.

The model tradition embraced it early. Max Bruckner photographed his paper model in Vielecke und Vielflache (1900, plate XI, fig. 24); Albert Harry Wheeler listed it as no. 11 in his 1924 Toronto congress paper on icosahedron forms; the Crennells' 1999 numbering of the fifty-nine makes it stellation 7. Magnus Wenninger's Polyhedron Models (1971) gives it as model W41 — the sixteenth of his seventeen icosahedron stellations, and among the most-built paper models in the book. Its dual is the great stellated dodecahedron, so the two Kepler-Poinsot solids that bracket the story — Kepler's last and Poinsot's last — are mirror partners under polarity.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner photographed his paper model of the great icosahedron in Vielecke und Vielflache (1900) on Tafel XI as Fig. 24 — the plate-and-figure reference still cited in the standard table of the fifty-nine stellations. By 1900 the solid was classical: Brückner's book, which surveys the theory and history of star polyhedra, presents it among the known stellations of the icosahedron while adding six icosahedron stellations of his own discovery elsewhere in the survey (per Guy Inchbald's history of stellation).

Five Cubes in a Dodecahedron (Cundy & Rollett, Mathematical Models, §3.10.6 in the 3rd edn)
regular compound of five cubes (one of the five regular polyhedral compounds)
info.catalog_ids: UC9 (Skilling 1976) · Coxeter 2{5,3}[5{4,3}] · Brückner §156, Taf. XII Fig. 24 · Cundy & Rollett §3.10.6 · dual: five octahedra (UC17, W23, Du Val C)
history: Choose eight of a regular dodecahedron's twenty vertices that form a cube. There are exactly five ways to do it, and taken together the five cubes use every vertex exactly twice: each pair of cubes shares one body diagonal of the dodecahedron (a threefold axis), and the compound's sixty edges are precisely the sixty diagonals of the twelve pentagonal faces — a pentagram inscribed in every face, each cube contributing one edge per pentagon. One such cube is ancient: Euclid closes the Elements (XIII.17) by constructing the dodecahedron around a cube, raising a pentagonal roof over each cube edge, so that every edge of the cube lies beneath a face as one of its diagonals. What the nineteenth century added was the idea of taking all five cubes at once as a single solid — the figure whose sixty rotations shuffle the five cubes in every even permutation, now the standard picture of why the icosahedral rotation group is the alternating group A5. A further coincidence: its sixty edges are exactly the edges of a uniform polyhedron, the small ditrigonal icosidodecahedron.

As a solid compound it is credited to Edmund Hess of Marburg in 1876. Wikipedia's articles on the regular compounds all state it was "first described by Edmund Hess in 1876", and Brückner's own footnotes identify the memoir he is drawing on: Über die zugleich gleicheckigen und gleichflächigen Polyeder (Kassel, 1876), which Brückner cites throughout as "Hess III". For its dual, the compound of five octahedra, there is a genuine priority dispute — Guy Inchbald's history of stellation argues that Cauchy already knew the compounds of five octahedra and of five and ten tetrahedra around 1812, since they fall out of his stellations of the icosahedron — but the dispute does not transfer to the five cubes: it is not a stellation of the icosahedron, and Inchbald's Cauchy entry pointedly lists the other three compounds without it. So among the icosahedral regular compounds the five cubes has the cleanest Hess pedigree, with one wrinkle: Inchbald's own timeline has no 1876 entry for Hess at all (his Hess entry is 1883), so the date rests on Wikipedia's articles and on Brückner's contemporary citation rather than on any modern critical study. I found no earlier drawing — Jamnitzer's 1568 Perspectiva Corporum Regularium, rich in stellated forms, does not appear to contain it.

The other way to see it is Brückner's way: the thirty square faces lie in the thirty face planes of the rhombic triacontahedron, so the intersection of the five cubes is exactly the triacontahedron and their union is one of its stellations — the most famous member of an enormous family (G. S. Pawley counted 227 "non-reentrant" stellations of the triacontahedron in 1975; Peter Messer enumerated 228 fully supported ones in 1995). Brückner read the compound off the complete figure of the triacontahedron's planes in 1900 and photographed his paper model on plate XII; from there it became perhaps the best-loved compound in the model-building tradition. Cundy and Rollett's Mathematical Models (first published 1952) taught generations to build it as "Five Cubes in a Dodecahedron", ideally in five colours, one per cube; John Skilling's 1976 census of uniform compounds catalogued it as UC9; and Hugo Verheyen's Symmetry Orbits (2007) photographs intricate paper models by Verheyen and Magnus Wenninger. George Hart calls it the "standard" compound of five cubes, "noteworthy for creating so much symmetry out of just five pieces".

The Escher connection turns out to be a near miss, and worth stating carefully. Escher knew Brückner's Vielecke und Vielflache and, per George Hart, based much of his knowledge of stellated polyhedra and compounds on it. But in the wood engraving Stars (1948) and the woodcut Study for Stars (August 1948) the compounds actually identified by Hart's survey and Wikipedia's inventory are the compound of three octahedra (the central cage), a stella octangula, a compound of cube and octahedron, and a compound of two cubes on a common threefold axis — the five-cube compound appears in neither work, and I found no Escher piece that uses it. The two-cube star is at least its germ: inside the five-cube compound, any two of the cubes form just such a figure, sharing a single body diagonal along a threefold axis. If Escher ever met the five cubes, it would have been on Brückner's plate XII, two plates past the ones he mined for Stars and Waterfall; there is no evidence he drew it.
info.bruckner_context: Brückner derives it, rather than merely picturing it. In §153 (p. 206) he builds "die vollständige Figur" — the complete figure of the icosahedron's twenty face planes, his stellation diagram, footnoted twice to "Hess III", i.e. Hess's Kassel memoir of 1876 — and reads the five octahedra and the five- and ten-tetrahedra compounds straight off it; §156 (p. 209) repeats the construction for the thirty planes of the rhombic triacontahedron, and there the reciprocal of the five octahedra, the compound of five cubes, emerges as a stellation of the triacontahedron. The paper model is photographed as Fig. 24 of Taf. XII (lower right of the plate). In this project's cell model that solid is exactly the union of the triacontahedron's first five shells, cells {0,1,2,3,4}.
